source_title: Vegetable Production Guide — Korogwe, Tanga, Tanzania

chunks.text: Tomato varieties for Korogwe: Improved varieties: Tanya VF (hybrid, 70 days to maturity, determinate, 8-12 tons per acre, resistant to bacterial wilt and fusarium), Cal-J (hybrid, 75 days, indeterminate, high yield 10-15 tons, good for fresh market), Roma VF (determinate, 75 days, 6-10 tons, good for processing and paste making), Money Maker (open pollinated, 80 days, 5-8 tons, widely adapted). Tomato planting: two seasons — long rains (February-March for transplant) and short rains (August-September). Seedling production: sow in nursery bed 4-6 weeks before transplant, transplant when 10-15cm tall with 4-5 true leaves. Spacing: 60cm x 60cm (11,000 plants per acre) for determinate types, 75cm x 60cm for indeterminate. Staking: essential for indeterminate types, use 1.5m wooden stakes. Fertilizer: 100 kg DAP at planting, top dress with 50 kg CAN at flowering, 50 kg CAN at fruiting. Pruning: remove suckers below first flower cluster for indeterminate types. Common tomato diseases: early blight (Alternaria solani), late blight (Phytophthora infestans), bacterial wilt (Ralstonia solanacearum), tomato leaf curl virus (transmitted by whitefly).

Kale (Sukuma Wiki) production for Korogwe: Varieties: Thousand Head (open pollinated, 60-75 days to first harvest, continuous harvest for 6-12 months, 5-8 tons per acre), Mfalme (hybrid, 50-60 days, 8-12 tons, dark green leaves, slow to bolt), Ethiopian kale (Brassica carinata, heat tolerant, 45-60 days, 4-6 tons, drought tolerant). Planting: can plant year-round in Korogwe due to warm climate, best during short rains (October-December) when pest pressure is lower. Direct sow or transplant: spacing 30cm x 30cm (44,000 plants per acre). Fertilizer: 50 kg DAP at planting, top dress with CAN every 3-4 weeks (25 kg per application). Harvest: begin cutting outer leaves when plant has 6-8 leaves (6-8 weeks after transplant), harvest 2-3 times per week, always leave growing point intact. Continues producing for 6-12 months if well managed. Pests: diamondback moth (Plutella xylostella) — most destructive, larvae chew holes in leaves, control: Bt spray, neem, or spinosad. Aphids — transmit virus diseases, control: dimethoate or neem. Diseases: black rot (Xanthomonas campestris), club root (Plasmodiophora brassicae) in waterlogged soils.

Onion production for Korogwe: Varieties: Red Creole (open pollinated, 90-120 days, 4-6 tons per acre, good storage, red bulb), Bombay Red (90-100 days, 3-5 tons, pungent, good for local market), Texas Grano (100-120 days, 5-8 tons, large bulb, mild flavour). Planting: raise seedlings in nursery (sow 8-10 weeks before transplant), transplant when pencil-thick (6-8 weeks). Planting seasons: long rains transplant in March-April, short rains transplant in September-October. Spacing: 15cm x 10cm (267,000 plants per acre) for small bulbs, 20cm x 15cm for large bulbs. Fertilizer: 100 kg DAP at planting, top dress with 50 kg CAN at 4 weeks and 50 kg CAN at 8 weeks. Onions are heavy feeders — respond well to well-decomposed manure (5 tons per acre). Irrigation: onions need consistent moisture, especially during bulb formation (weeks 6-12), reduce watering 2 weeks before harvest to promote curing. Pests: thrips (Thrips tabaci) — most damaging, causes silvering of leaves, reduce bulb size, control: spray with dimethoate or spinosad every 7-10 days. Onion fly — larvae bore into bulbs, control: crop rotation. Diseases: purple blotch (Alternaria porri), downy mildew (Peronospora destructor), neck rot (Botrytis allii) in storage.

African leafy vegetables for Korogwe: Amaranth (Amaranthus spp) — fast growing 30-45 days to first harvest, heat tolerant, sow directly or transplant, spacing 20cm x 10cm, harvest leaves continuously, high in iron and calcium, 3-5 tons per acre. Spider plant (Cleome gynandra) — traditional leafy vegetable, 45-60 days, sow directly, thin to 15cm spacing, harvest whole plant or cut leaves, 2-4 tons per acre. Cowpea leaves (Vigna unguiculata) — harvest from 30 days after planting, dual purpose (leaves and grain), high protein, heat and drought tolerant, 1-2 tons leaves per acre in addition to grain. Ethiopian mustard (Brassica carinata) — heat tolerant brassica, 45-60 days, similar to kale but more drought tolerant, 3-5 tons per acre. Nightshade (Solanum nigrum) — traditional green, 30-45 days, self-seeding, harvest young leaves (mature leaves may contain solanine — avoid). Management: all these vegetables benefit from regular harvesting (promotes branching), light fertilizer application (25 kg CAN per acre every 3-4 weeks), and consistent moisture.

Watermelon production for Korogwe: Varieties: Sugar Baby (round, 80-90 days, 3-5 kg fruit, dark green rind, sweet red flesh), Charleston Gray (oblong, 90-100 days, 8-12 kg, light green rind), Crimson Sweet (round, 80-85 days, 6-10 kg, light green with dark stripes). Planting: plant at start of long rains (March) or short rains (October), spacing 2m x 1m (2,000 plants per acre) or 1.5m x 1m for smaller types. Direct sow 3-4 seeds per hole, thin to 1 plant per hole at 3-4 leaf stage. Fertilizer: 50 kg DAP at planting, side dress with 25 kg CAN at vine runner stage, 25 kg CAN at flowering. Watermelons need full sun and warm soil (minimum 20°C for germination). Irrigation: critical during flowering and fruit development, reduce watering as fruit ripens to increase sweetness. Pests: fruit flies (Dacus spp) — puncture fruit causing rot, control: bag developing fruit, spray with protein bait + spinosad. Aphids — transmit watermelon mosaic virus, control with dimethoate. Diseases: fusarium wilt (soil-borne, use resistant varieties), anthracnose (Colletotrichum orbiculare). Harvest: tap fruit — ripe watermelon sounds hollow, tendril nearest fruit dries brown, ground spot turns yellow, 80-100 days after planting.

Pumpkin and butternut squash for Korogwe: Varieties: Duma (local pumpkin, large fruit 5-15 kg, orange flesh, 90-120 days, good storage), Butternut Waltham (butternut, 85-95 days, 1-2 kg fruit, tan skin, sweet orange flesh, good storage 3-6 months). Planting: plant at start of rains, spacing 2m x 1.5m for pumpkins (1,300 plants per acre), 1.5m x 1m for butternut (2,600 plants per acre). Direct sow 2-3 seeds per hole, thin to 1. Fertilizer: 50 kg DAP at planting, side dress with CAN at flowering. Pumpkins tolerate poor soil but respond to fertility. Pests: fruit flies (same as watermelon), squash fly (Dacus ciliatus), red pumpkin beetle (Aulacophora foveicollis) — adults eat leaves and flowers, control: spray with lambda-cyhalothrin. Diseases: powdery mildew (common in dry conditions), downy mildew (wet conditions). Harvest: pumpkin when stem dries and skin resists thumbnail scratch (90-120 days), butternut when skin turns deep tan and stem dries (85-100 days). Cure in sun for 7-10 days after harvest. Storage: store in cool dry place, pumpkins keep 3-6 months, butternut 4-8 months.
